name: Kimura from Quarter Guard
summary: The Kimura from Quarter Guard is a figure-four shoulder lock applied from the dominant top passing position, attacking the bottom player's near arm with forced internal rotation as their underhook or framing attempts expose the wrist.
description: Master the Kimura shoulder lock from Quarter Guard top. Expert guide covering figure-four grip attacks, finishing mechanics, counters, and training drills for BJJ.
target_area: Shoulder joint, rotator cuff, and shoulder capsule
overview:
The Kimura from Quarter Guard exploits a unique positional advantage where the top player has nearly completed their guard pass, creating ideal conditions for the figure-four shoulder lock. Unlike attacking the Kimura from full half guard where the bottom player retains significant defensive capability, the quarter guard position compromises the defender's ability to maintain frames and creates accessible angles for wrist isolation. The top player's advanced hip position and crossface pressure naturally funnel the bottom player's arms into vulnerable configurations, particularly when they reach for underhooks or attempt to frame against the pass.

This submission capitalizes on the bottom player's defensive urgency. As they fight to retain guard with diminishing control, their near arm becomes exposed through framing attempts or underhook battles. The top player can transition seamlessly from passing pressure to kimura grip, using the same crossface and weight distribution that drives the pass to control the submission setup. The figure-four configuration locks the shoulder in internal rotation while the top player's body weight prevents escape, creating a high-percentage finish that chains naturally with guard passing sequences.

The Kimura from Quarter Guard is particularly effective because it punishes the bottom player's primary defensive tool—the underhook. When the defender commits their arm to the underhook seeking sweeps or back takes, they expose the exact wrist and forearm angles needed for the figure-four grip. This creates a tactical dilemma where the bottom player must choose between defending the pass without their strongest tool or risking the submission by fighting for the underhook.

injury_risks.injury: Rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis)

injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 weeks for strain, 3-6 months for rupture

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training, allowing partner time to recognize danger and tap
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or making any verbal distress sound)
Physical hand tap (multiple taps with free hand)
Physical foot tap (multiple taps with either foot)
Any distress signal including screaming or unusual sounds
release_protocol: Immediately stop all rotational pressure the instant tap is felt or heard
Return the arm toward neutral position (externally rotate back to starting position)
Allow partner to self-assess shoulder mobility before continuing
Never release suddenly or allow arm to spring back forcefully
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the submission - rotation must be smooth and controlled
Never use competition speed or surprise attacks in training
Always ensure partner has at least one hand free to tap
Do not apply while partner is in awkward body position that prevents tapping
Never combine with weight pressure that restricts breathing while finishing
Respect immediate taps without testing partner's pain tolerance

attacker.name: Kimura from Quarter Guard Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the Kimura from Quarter Guard top position. Step-by-step execution guide covering grip mechanics, finishing details, counter responses, and progressive training methods.
attacker.overview: Attacking the Kimura from Quarter Guard requires integrating submission mechanics with passing pressure. The top player must recognize the moment when the bottom player's arm becomes vulnerable—typically during underhook attempts or framing sequences—and transition smoothly from pass-focused pressure to figure-four grip control. The key advantage of this position is that your weight distribution and crossface already restrict the defender's escape options, allowing you to focus on wrist isolation and rotational finishing mechanics rather than fighting for positional control. The quarter guard creates a natural funnel where the bottom player's defensive arm movements expose the exact angles needed for kimura entry, making this one of the highest-percentage submission setups available during guard passing sequences.
key_principles: Control the wrist before committing to the figure-four—premature grip attempts telegraph your intention and allow preemptive defense
Maintain crossface pressure throughout the kimura setup to prevent the bottom player from turning into you or creating defensive frames
Pin the captured elbow tight against your hip to create a fixed fulcrum point, maximizing rotational leverage while minimizing escape angles
Use your body weight and hip rotation to drive the finish rather than arm strength—the kimura is a whole-body submission, not an arm crank
Keep your base low and wide during the finishing sequence to resist the bottom player's bridge and roll escape attempts
Attack the arm during transitions—the moment the bottom player extends for an underhook or frame is the highest-percentage entry window
setup_requirements: Established quarter guard top position with crossface control preventing opponent from turning into you
Bottom player's near arm exposed through underhook attempt, frame, or failed grip fighting
Your hips advanced past opponent's centerline with weight distributed forward through chest and shoulder
Free hand available to secure wrist control while maintaining positional pressure through shoulder weight
Opponent's far shoulder pinned to mat through crossface, limiting their ability to rotate away from the attack

execution_steps.description: From established quarter guard top with crossface pressure, watch for the bottom player's near arm extending as they reach for an underhook, create a frame against your chest, or attempt to push against your hip. This momentary extension creates the grip access needed for the kimura entry.
execution_steps.timing: Immediate recognition within 1-2 seconds of arm exposure

execution_steps.action: Secure wrist control with far hand
execution_steps.description: Release your far-side hand from hip control and grip the bottom player's exposed wrist using a C-grip with your thumb pointing toward their fingers. Maintain shoulder pressure through crossface to compensate for releasing the hip control grip during this transition.

Slide your crossface-side arm underneath the bottom player's trapped forearm from the outside, threading between their arm and their torso. Connect your threading hand to your own wrist that holds their wrist, establishing the complete figure-four configuration with your forearm pressing against the back of theirs.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds for clean threading without rushing

execution_steps.action: Pin the elbow to your hip
execution_steps.description: Drive the bottom player's captured elbow tight against your hip bone using the figure-four grip, creating a fixed fulcrum point. This pinning action prevents them from straightening the arm and establishes the mechanical advantage needed for rotational finishing pressure.

Shift your body weight slightly toward the bottom player's head while keeping your chest heavy on their upper body. This angle adjustment opens the rotational path needed to drive their wrist toward the mat while maintaining control over their torso and preventing escape.

Using hip rotation and body weight rather than arm strength alone, drive the bottom player's wrist in a paintbrush arc toward the mat down by their hip and lower back, behind their body. Maintain the elbow pin throughout the rotation as the shoulder enters progressively deeper internal rotation toward the submission finish.
execution_steps.timing: 3-5 seconds of slow progressive rotation in training

execution_steps.action: Complete the finish and release on tap
execution_steps.description: Continue smooth progressive rotational pressure until the opponent taps. Keep your base wide and weight heavy through the final phase to resist any last-attempt bridge escapes. Release immediately upon feeling or hearing the tap signal and return the arm gently to neutral position.

common_counters.counter: Straighten the arm to prevent figure-four lock from closing
common_counters.your_response: Maintain wrist grip and use chest pressure to drive the arm back into bent position, or transition to straight armbar since their extended arm is now vulnerable to hyperextension

common_counters.counter: Grab own shorts or belt with trapped hand to anchor wrist against rotation
common_counters.your_response: Increase chest pressure to limit anchoring capability, then use circular figure-four motion at changing angles the grip cannot sustain, or bump their gripping hand free with your knee

common_counters.counter: Bridge and roll toward the trapped arm to disrupt base and break grip
common_counters.your_response: Widen base by stepping far leg out and dropping weight through chest onto upper body to flatten opponent back down, or follow the roll direction maintaining grip to finish from new angle

common_counters.counter: Turn aggressively into attacker to reduce available rotational angle
common_counters.your_response: Increase crossface pressure to flatten them back or follow their rotation to maintain the finishing angle, adjusting your hip position to preserve the rotational path as they turn

common_errors.error: Releasing crossface to grab the wrist with both hands simultaneously
common_errors.consequence: Opponent turns into you immediately, creates defensive frames, and escapes the quarter guard position entirely
common_errors.correction: Keep crossface shoulder heavy while far hand secures wrist first, then thread the crossface arm for the figure-four while maintaining shoulder pressure through body weight

common_errors.error: Lifting captured elbow away from body during the rotational finish
common_errors.consequence: Reduces mechanical leverage dramatically and allows the opponent to extract their arm by straightening against the weakened figure-four
common_errors.correction: Keep the captured elbow pinned tightly against your hip bone throughout the entire finishing sequence, using it as the fixed fulcrum point for all rotation

common_errors.error: Pulling the wrist with arm strength instead of using body rotation and weight
common_errors.consequence: Fatigues quickly, gives opponent time to organize defense, and produces inconsistent finishing pressure that experienced defenders can resist
common_errors.correction: Drive the finish through hip rotation and body weight shift, letting your torso movement power the wrist arc rather than muscling with your arms

common_errors.error: Attacking before securing proper wrist control with confirmed C-grip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent strips the grip easily during the threading phase and becomes defensively aware, making subsequent attempts significantly harder
common_errors.correction: Confirm solid wrist grip with thumb toward their fingers before committing to the figure-four transition, ensuring you have purchase before the arm thread

common_errors.error: Neglecting base during the finishing sequence by focusing entirely on the grip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent bridges and rolls successfully, reversing position and escaping from what should be a secured submission
common_errors.correction: Maintain wide base with far leg posted and hips low throughout the finish, distributing weight across the opponent's upper body while applying rotation

common_errors.error: Rushing the rotation at competition speed during training
common_errors.consequence: Risks serious shoulder injury to training partner including rotator cuff tears and labral damage requiring months of recovery
common_errors.correction: Apply rotation over three to five seconds minimum in training, giving partner clear time to recognize the danger and tap before the shoulder reaches its limit

flashcards.question: What anatomical structure does the Kimura from Quarter Guard primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The Kimura primarily attacks the shoulder joint, specifically targeting the rotator cuff complex including the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis muscles, the glenoid labrum, and the shoulder capsule through forced internal rotation that exceeds the joint's natural range of motion.

flashcards.question: Your opponent straightens their arm as you attempt the figure-four grip—what adjustment do you make?
flashcards.answer: Maintain your wrist grip and use chest pressure to drive their arm back into the bent position by pressing your body weight forward. If they resist the rebend, transition to a straight armbar opportunity since their extended arm is now vulnerable to hyperextension attacks from your dominant quarter guard top position.

flashcards.question: What are the critical control points that must be established before attempting the kimura rotation?
flashcards.answer: Before attempting rotation, you must have a secure figure-four grip locked around their wrist and forearm, their elbow pinned tightly against your hip creating the fulcrum, crossface or shoulder pressure preventing their body from turning into you, and your base positioned wide enough to resist bridge escape attempts during the finishing sequence.

flashcards.question: How does the quarter guard position create unique advantages for the kimura compared to standard half guard top?
flashcards.answer: Quarter guard provides superior kimura opportunities because your hips have advanced past the opponent's centerline, giving you more weight distribution over their upper body. The bottom player's compromised position forces them to use their arms more aggressively for frames and underhooks, creating frequent arm exposure windows. Their reduced leg control also limits the hip movement needed for effective bridge escapes during the finish.

plausible: More leg control than half guard
trap: Faster guard pass, skip the arm

flashcards.question: Your opponent bridges toward the trapped arm during the finishing sequence—how do you maintain control?
flashcards.answer: Widen your base by stepping your far leg out while keeping your near knee tight to their hip. Drop your weight heavily through your chest onto their upper body to flatten them back down. If the bridge continues despite weight adjustment, follow the roll direction and maintain the grip—you can finish the kimura from the resulting position or transition to side control with the grip intact.
flashcards.answer_line: Widen base, drop chest to flatten

plausible: Sit up tall to ride the bridge

flashcards.question: What grip adjustments should you make if your opponent's wrist becomes difficult to control during rotation?
flashcards.answer: Deepen the figure-four by sliding your gripping hand further past their wrist toward their forearm, increasing the contact surface area for control. Squeeze your elbows together to compress the grip configuration. If the grip continues slipping, pause the rotation and reposition your hands with a fresh grip before continuing rather than rushing the finish with compromised control.

flashcards.question: When should you immediately release the Kimura during training, and what is the proper release sequence?
flashcards.answer: Release immediately upon any tap signal—verbal, hand tap, foot tap, or any distress sound. The release sequence is: stop all rotational pressure instantly, return the wrist toward neutral by externally rotating back to starting position, release the figure-four grip completely, and allow your partner to self-assess shoulder mobility before continuing. Never release suddenly or let the arm spring back forcefully.

plausible: Let go of grip instantly, walk off
Hold position and ask if okay
trap: Let the arm spring back fast

flashcards.question: What is the point of no escape for the defender, and how do you recognize when the submission is secured?
flashcards.answer: The point of no escape occurs when the elbow is pinned firmly to your hip, the figure-four is fully locked with both wrists secured, and rotation has passed approximately forty-five degrees of internal rotation. Indicators include the opponent's body beginning to twist involuntarily with the rotation, their free hand switching from grip fighting to preparing to tap, and audible distress signals. Once past this point, apply remaining pressure slowly.

trap: Wait for a verbal tap only

flashcards.question: Your opponent grabs their own shorts to anchor against the rotation—how do you break this defense?
flashcards.answer: Address the shorts grip by first increasing your chest pressure to limit their ability to maintain the anchor. Then use a circular motion with the figure-four, arcing the wrist in a wider circle that creates changing angles the static shorts grip cannot sustain. You can also bump their gripping hand free with your knee or hip. If the grip persists, consider transitioning to an americana by switching the rotational direction.

plausible: Wait for them to release it
trap: Rip their hand off the shorts

flashcards.question: How do you manage the transition from crossface control to kimura grip without losing positional dominance?
flashcards.answer: Maintain shoulder pressure through the crossface side even as your hands transition to the kimura grip. Your shoulder should stay heavy on their face or far cheek throughout the transition using body weight rather than hand control. Secure the wrist with your far hand first before moving your crossface arm, then thread the figure-four arm quickly while your shoulder maintains pressure through positioning.

trap: Lift chest to muscle the grip

defender.name: Kimura from Quarter Guard Defender
defender.description: Defend against the Kimura from Quarter Guard. Learn recognition cues, grip breaking, escape techniques, and recovery strategies to survive this shoulder lock attack.
defender.overview: Defending the Kimura from Quarter Guard demands early recognition and immediate grip prevention, as the compromised quarter guard position already limits your mobility and framing options significantly. The defender must balance the need to maintain underhook control for sweeps with the risk of exposing their arm to the figure-four grip. Successful defense requires understanding the attacker's grip sequence and intervening before the figure-four locks fully, using body rotation, grip fighting, and guard recovery to neutralize the threat before the shoulder enters dangerous rotation. The quarter guard bottom position adds urgency because your reduced leg engagement means you cannot generate the powerful hip escapes available from full half guard, making early grip prevention far more important than late-stage escape attempts.
key_principles: Recognize the kimura threat early—once the figure-four is fully locked, escape difficulty increases dramatically with each passing second
Keep elbows tight to your body to deny the wrist exposure needed for the initial C-grip control
Fight the grip before it locks completely—breaking a partial figure-four is far easier than escaping a completed one
Use hip rotation toward the attacker to reduce the rotational angle available for the finishing sequence
Maintain at least one grip break option at all times, keeping your free hand ready to fight the figure-four or anchor your wrist
Bridge timing is critical—bridge toward the trapped arm before rotation begins, not during the finish when the attacker's leverage is maximal
recognition_cues: Opponent's far hand releases position control and reaches toward your near wrist or forearm instead of maintaining hip pressure
Crossface pressure shifts as opponent begins threading their arm under your trapped arm for the figure-four configuration
Sudden weight shift toward your head combined with your elbow being driven toward the opponent's hip bone
Opponent abandons passing momentum and redirects attention specifically to controlling and isolating your near arm

defensive_options.action: Straighten arm and pull elbow tight to ribs to deny bent-arm configuration
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately when you feel the opponent's hand gripping your wrist before the figure-four threads
defensive_options.if_successful: Denies the kimura entry completely and forces opponent to return to passing
defensive_options.risk: Extended arm may be vulnerable to straight armbar if opponent transitions

defensive_options.action: Bridge toward trapped arm side and roll through to break the figure-four grip
defensive_options.when_to_use: After the figure-four is locked but before significant rotation has started
defensive_options.if_successful: Breaks the grip through momentum and recovers to half guard or creates a scramble
defensive_options.risk: If bridge is weak or mistimed, opponent can follow the roll and finish the kimura from the new angle

defensive_options.action: Turn body aggressively into the attacker to reduce available rotational angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: During any phase where the opponent's base is compromised or weight is shifted forward
defensive_options.if_successful: Eliminates the rotational path needed for the finish and creates guard recovery opportunity
defensive_options.risk: Turning in may expose your back if the opponent abandons the kimura and takes back control

defensive_options.action: Grab own wrist with free hand to create two-on-one anchor against rotation
defensive_options.when_to_use: When figure-four is locked and you cannot straighten the arm or bridge effectively
defensive_options.if_successful: Stalls the rotation and buys time to set up bridge escape or guard recovery
defensive_options.risk: Temporary measure only—attacker can break the wrist grip with persistent pressure and angle changes

escape_paths: Straighten the captured arm powerfully and pull elbow tight to your ribcage, breaking the figure-four configuration before rotation can begin
Bridge toward the trapped arm side and roll through using momentum to break the grip and recover half guard position
Turn aggressively into the attacker while pulling the arm free, reducing rotational angle and creating space to recover guard

favorable_outcomes.how: Bridge and roll when attacker overcommits weight to the finish, using their grip attachment against them to disrupt base and recover to half guard with improved defensive position

common_errors.error: Reaching aggressively for underhooks without protecting wrist position
common_errors.consequence: Creates the exact arm exposure the top player needs for the kimura C-grip entry, turning your primary offensive tool into a submission vulnerability
common_errors.correction: Reach for underhooks with awareness of wrist position, keeping your elbow bent and close to your body until the underhook is fully secured rather than extending with a straight arm

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to defend hoping the kimura attempt will fail on its own
common_errors.consequence: Once rotation begins with proper elbow pin, escape probability drops below twenty percent and injury risk increases with each degree of rotation
common_errors.correction: Defend immediately upon recognizing the grip threat—fight the wrist control, straighten the arm, or bridge before the figure-four fully locks rather than after

common_errors.error: Pulling straight back against the figure-four direction to escape
common_errors.consequence: Fighting directly against the figure-four leverage accelerates the internal rotation and can cause sudden shoulder injury before you can tap
common_errors.correction: Turn your body into the attacker or bridge toward the trapped arm to reduce the angle rather than pulling directly against the submission's mechanical advantage

common_errors.error: Using the free arm to push the attacker's body away instead of fighting the grip
common_errors.consequence: Exposes the free arm to secondary attacks while removing your best grip-fighting tool from the primary defense
common_errors.correction: Keep your free hand connected to your trapped wrist for anchoring or actively fighting the figure-four grip rather than pushing against the attacker's torso

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that a Kimura from Quarter Guard is being set up before the grip locks?
flashcards.answer: Key recognition cues include the top player's far hand releasing hip control and reaching toward your near wrist, a shift in their pressure from passing-focused to arm-isolation-focused, their crossface arm beginning to thread underneath your forearm, and sudden attention to controlling your near arm rather than advancing the pass. Any time the top player abandons passing momentum to focus on your arm, assume a kimura attack is developing.
flashcards.answer_line: Far hand attacks your near wrist

plausible: They suddenly speed up the pass
They switch to a collar grip

flashcards.question: What is the safest response when you feel the figure-four grip beginning to close around your wrist?
flashcards.answer: The safest immediate response is to straighten your arm powerfully while pulling your elbow tight to your ribcage, denying the bent-arm configuration the kimura requires. If the grip is already partially locked, use your free hand to grip your own wrist and fight to straighten the arm. Never try to muscle out by rotating against the submission direction as this accelerates injury risk. Tap immediately if rotation begins and you cannot break the grip.

flashcards.question: At what point should you tap to the Kimura from Quarter Guard to prevent injury?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel the shoulder rotation passing the point where you can actively resist or reverse the submission. Specific indicators include sharp or increasing pain in the shoulder joint, inability to prevent further rotation despite maximum effort, and feeling your shoulder forced past its comfortable range of motion. In training, tap early—the shoulder is vulnerable to injuries requiring months of recovery and potentially surgery. Never wait to test your limits once significant rotation has begun.
flashcards.answer_line: At first sharp pain or forced stall

plausible: Only once you can't move at all

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available once the figure-four is fully locked but rotation has not started?
flashcards.answer: With the figure-four locked pre-rotation, your best options are: bridge toward the trapped arm side to disrupt the attacker's base and potentially roll through; grab your own wrist with your free hand to fight straightening the arm; turn your body aggressively into the attacker to reduce the available rotational angle; or use your legs to hook the attacker's leg and create leverage for a bridge escape. These options diminish rapidly once rotation begins.
flashcards.answer_line: Bridge toward the trapped arm side

plausible: Bridge away from the trapped arm
Pull straight to yank it out

flashcards.question: What common mistake causes defenders to get caught by the Kimura from Quarter Guard most frequently?
flashcards.answer: The most common mistake is overcommitting to the underhook without protecting the wrist. Practitioners focus so intently on establishing the underhook for sweeps and back takes that they extend their arm carelessly, creating the exact wrist exposure the top player needs. The correction is to reach for the underhook with awareness of your wrist position, keeping your elbow bent and close to your body until the underhook is fully secured rather than reaching with an extended arm.

plausible: Rushing the back take too early
trap: Turning away to hide the arm
